Thus, quantum dot photodetectors should experience fewer changes in carriers available for excitation, allowing their performance to be stable throughout a larger range of temperatures. A lower dark current is also expected due to the small area overlap of the Fermi distribution function and the 0D density of states, allowing for higher operating temperatures than QW photodetectors.

The research reported here is part of an extensive investigation of quantum dot infrared photodetectors (QDIPs), conducted at the Center for Qunatum Devices (CQD).⁶ The overall goal of the group is to improve the performance of QDIP devices made at CQD, including increasing their detectivity and lowering their dark current. Two teams were formed, each working with their own low-pressure metalorganic vapor deposition (LP MOCVD) reactors. These teams subdivided into more focused areas, including theory, III/V semiconductor material properties, and device processing. After completing extensive background research on the work of other research groups investigating quantum dots, a material system was chosen to start each segment of the research. Next, quantum dots were grown and optimized with the chosen material system for a device structure. After device processing, each sample was tested and compared to previous results.

The material system chosen for QDIP research is an InGaAs/InGaP structure on a semi-insulating InP substrate, grown by a LP MOCVD reactor (see Fig3). A 0.5μm GaAs contact layer doped to n = 1×10¹⁸ cm⁻³ was first grown on the GaAs substrate, followed by a 0.1μm InGaP barrier layer. Next, 10 layers of n-type doped GaInAs quantum dots were grown, with an InGaP barrier layer between each quantum dot layer. Multiple layers were grown in order to increase the overall efficiency of the device by providing more area for photon absorption. This structure is completed with a .5μm GaAs top contact layer doped to n = 1×10¹⁸ cm⁻³.

Before this device structure was grown, the optimal growth condition for the quantum dots was found by changing the reactor’s growth parameters such as growth rate, V/III ratio, and growth temperature. The quantum dots were grown through a self-assembly

epitaxial growth technique known as the Stranski-Krastanow growth mode.⁷,⁸ This method utilizes the strain produced between two materials of different lattice parameters to grow small islands of strained material, or quantum dots. The optimal growth rate, V/III ratio, and temperature for the InGaAs quantum dots grown on InGaP were found to be 0.68 ML/s, 480, and 440°C, respectively. The InGaAs/InGaP QDIP structure described above was tested using a Fourier transform infrared spectrometer, which gave a peak photoresponse at 4.7μm with a cutoff wavelength of 5.2μm. This response peak did not change considerably with a change in temperature form T = 30K to T = 140K, showing the predicted insensitivity of quantum dots with varying temperature. The device had a very high responsivity of 3.1 A/W at T=95K and a bias voltage of –5V, as shown in Figure 5. A low dark current was observed in the QDIP device, which was 0.98 pA at T = 120K at a bias of 0.1V (Fig.6). This observation shows the predicted low dark current for quantum dot devices. In addition, a high detectivity of 3.62×10¹⁰cm Hz¹ᐟ²/W at a bias of –1.4V at T = 95K was observed in the device. This is comparable to the performance of most QWIP devices around 100K.⁹,¹⁰
